title: Shannon's Sampling Theorem: Why Twice the Bandwidth?

paper.title: Communication in the Presence of Noise

hook: A sine wave sampled too slowly looks like a different, slower sine wave. This is aliasing. Shannon's theorem tells us exactly how fast we must sample to avoid it.

equation.caption: The apparent frequency after sampling. If f_s > 2f, then k=0 and f_a = f (no aliasing).

steps: Set signal frequency f = {{f}} Hz and sampling frequency f_s = {{fs}} Hz.
If f_s > f_N, no aliasing: f_a = f = {{f}} Hz.
If f_s < f_N, aliasing occurs: f_a = |f - k f_s| with k = round(f/f_s).
Here k = round({{f}}/{{fs}}) and f_a = {{fa}} Hz.

explorations.title: No aliasing above Nyquist
explorations.predict: If f_s is greater than 2f, what is the apparent frequency?
explorations.observe: The reconstructed wave matches the original. f_a = 3 Hz.
explorations.why: When f_s > 2f, k = round(f/f_s) = 0, so f_a = |f - 0| = f. The samples capture the true oscillation.

explorations.title: Aliasing below Nyquist
explorations.predict: If f_s is less than 2f, what apparent frequency do you see?
explorations.observe: The reconstructed wave has a lower frequency than the original. f_a = 3 Hz.
explorations.why: Here k = round(7/10) = 1, so f_a = |7 - 1*10| = 3 Hz. The samples are consistent with a 3 Hz sine wave.

self_tests.name: Nyquist rate is twice signal frequency

limitation: This demonstration uses a single sine wave, but Shannon's theorem applies to any bandlimited signal. For a general signal with bandwidth B, the sampling rate must exceed 2B, and reconstruction requires an ideal low-pass filter (sinc interpolation), which is not shown here.
misconception: A common mistake is to think that sampling at exactly twice the highest frequency is sufficient. In practice, sampling must be strictly greater than twice the highest frequency to avoid aliasing, and real systems sample well above the Nyquist rate.

claims.text: A signal must be sampled at a rate greater than twice its highest frequency to be reconstructed without aliasing.
When sampling below the Nyquist rate, the apparent frequency is |f - k f_s| where k is the nearest integer to f/f_s.
The toy model uses a single sine wave and ideal sampling, ignoring quantization and filter effects.

outcomes.outcome: Explain why the sampling rate must exceed twice the highest frequency.
Predict the apparent frequency when aliasing occurs.
Verify that sampling above the Nyquist rate recovers the true frequency.
